title: Full fathom five: Ariel's song
short: Ariel sings to Ferdinand in The Tempest 1.2, telling him his father Alonso has drowned; Palgrave titled it 'A Sea Dirge'.
body: In The Tempest (c. 1611), act 1 scene 2, the invisible spirit Ariel, serving Prospero, leads the shipwrecked prince Ferdinand across the island with songs. This one tells him that his father, King Alonso of Naples, lies drowned; Ferdinand responds that 'the ditty does remember my drowned father'. In fact Alonso is alive, so the song is a fiction serving Prospero's design. The title 'A Sea Dirge' was given by F. T. Palgrave in The Golden Treasury (1861), the source of this text. A fathom is six feet, so the body lies thirty feet down.

title: thy father lies
short: 'Lies' means lies dead under the sea; since Alonso is alive, the line is also untrue, a dramatic irony.
body: The audience will discover that Alonso survived the shipwreck, so Ariel's dirge is consolingly false. The song's comfort, that the dead are transformed rather than destroyed, prepares for the play's pattern of apparent loss and recovery, in which the 'sea-change' happens to the living (Alonso's repentance, Ferdinand's love for Miranda). Editors have stressed how the song's beauty and its untruth work together.

anchor: Of his bones are coral made
title: Of his bones are coral made
short: The drowned man's bones are turned to coral and his eyes to pearls: decay pictured as transformation into precious things.
body: The image transforms the horror of decomposition into a jewel-like metamorphosis. Coral and pearl are both sea-born and precious, and both were thought to form by hardening. The verse is trochaic (stressed syllable first) and largely seven-syllable, as in many of Shakespeare's songs for spirits and fairies. The inversion 'Of his bones are coral made' stresses the bones and the change.

title: Those are pearls that were his eyes
short: A line quoted twice in T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922), where the drowned Phoenician sailor recalls the song.
body: Eliot quotes this line in 'The Burial of the Dead' (l. 48), in Madame Sosostris's tarot reading of 'the drowned Phoenician Sailor', and again in 'A Game of Chess' (l. 125). In Eliot's poem the Tempest's promise of transformation through death is set against modern sterility. The line has thus become a modernist touchstone as well as one of the best known in Shakespeare's songs.

title: suffer a sea-change
short: 'Suffer' means undergo; 'sea-change', a change wrought by the sea, was given its later idiomatic sense of total transformation by this line.
body: 'Suffer' means undergo, not necessarily with pain. A 'sea-change' is literally a change caused by the sea; this passage is the OED's earliest example of the compound, and the idiom of a profound transformation derives from it. 'Nothing of him that doth fade' means 'no part of him that is perishable but undergoes'. The phrase captures the play's concern with metamorphosis and redemption.

title: Into something rich and strange
short: The transformed dead become precious and marvellous; lines 4-6 are inscribed on Shelley's grave in Rome.
body: 'Rich' means precious, and 'strange' means wonderful and foreign. Percy Bysshe Shelley drowned in 1822 in the Gulf of La Spezia; his ashes were buried by Edward Trelawny in the Protestant Cemetery in Rome, and his gravestone bears the lines 'Nothing of him that doth fade, / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange'. The quotation, chosen for a drowned poet, shows how the song came to stand for the transforming power of art over death.

title: Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell
short: The sea-nymphs toll a funeral bell for him every hour, as a church bell tolls for the dead.
body: A 'knell' is the bell tolled at a death or funeral. Classical sea-nymphs (Nereids) are given an English parish custom, the passing bell. 'Hourly' suggests unending mourning. The juxtaposition of pagan nymphs and Christian bell typifies the play's mixed world. The bell motif is completed by the 'ding, dong' of the burden. Editors also note that 'hourly' may suggest the regular ringing of a church clock as well as perpetual mourning, and that the passing bell was rung as a person died, asking prayers for the soul.

title: Ding, dong, Bell
short: The burden or refrain, sung in the play by spirits off-stage; Robert Johnson's setting survives in a 1659 printed collection.
body: In the First Folio the song has a 'Burthen: ding dong', a refrain sung by invisible spirits, after which Ariel sings 'Hark, now I hear them, ding dong bell'. A setting by Robert Johnson, lutenist to the King's Men, was printed in John Wilson's Cheerfull Ayres (Oxford, 1659), and is possibly the music used in early performances. The onomatopoeia imitates the knell of the previous line.
